  • Kazakhstan Identifies Adaptation Planning and Reporting GapsThe document identifies institutional, data, coordination and staffing barriers to adaptation planning and reporting, which it says will be addressed through the Environmental Code and adopted plans and programmes.Concern0 points1 document1 quote

    The document identifies gaps in adaptation planning, monitoring and reporting: inadequate institutional and technical support for mainstreaming, no permanent cross-ministry and cross-region discussion platform, incomplete climate-information inventories, fragmented and outdated vulnerability assessments, a need to harmonize data methods, and insufficient trained personnel. It says these gaps will be addressed through the Environmental Code and adopted plans and programmes.

      “Existing gaps and barriers to climate change adaptation (CCA) planning, monitoring, and reporting in Kazakhstan comprise insufficient institutional and technical support for mainstreaming adaptation into sectoral and local development plans, lack of permanent inter-ministerial and cross-regional platform for discussion of adaptation issues, lack of inventories of existing climate information, combined with fragmented and outdated vulnerability assessments, strong need to harmonize techniques for climate-related data collection, analysis and documentation, lack of required trained personnel (numbers and expertise) to meet adaptation objectives. These gaps and barriers will be addressed in the course of implementing the provisions of the Environmental Code and in the process of implementing the adopted programs and plans.”

      “Achievement of NDC targets and carbon neutrality will demand holistic digitalization first of all in the energy sector and the environment to track a carbon footprint and to ensure transparency as well as the creation of an innovation ecosystem both for applied research programs and new financial tools on decarbonization. Key thematic areas, and research relevant to the Republic of Kazakhstan based on the R&D portfolio management approach, identifying promising topics and screening out low-impact projects. 2. competencies, courses and programs of formal education for the needs of decarbonization, and options for implementing digital multidisciplinary postgraduate education programs, including in partnership with foreign universities and online education platforms. 3. ways for integration and cooperation of organizations and industry with universities, by funding research programmes fellowships, setting up research centres focussing on sustainable development and carbon neutrality to prepare highly experienced personnel and carry out studies and research on decarbonization, taking into account the national circumstances. 4. approaches for creating an ecosystem for the development of new decarbonization solutions, including startup incubators and (or) integration with the existing ones.”

    • p. 17Text matched
      “Afforestation and reforestation mitigation outcomes under three different scenarios until 2030 were modelled with the use of CBM-CFS3 (Carbon Budget Model of the Canadian Forest Sector) software. In the first three years [after planting] each hectare of coniferous, soft-wooded, or hardwood trees absorbs the average of 1 ton of carbon per year that is equivalent to 3.67 tons of CO2 per year per hectare subject to lack of disturbances. However, later this parameter drops to 0.7 tons of carbon per year per forest hectare. This can be explained by forest aging which is leading to a decrease in carbon dioxide absorption. The 25-year lifespan of commercial forests will provide the country with adaptation benefits (water retention, wood for construction, etc.) as well as increase carbon sinks offsetting anthropogenic emissions that cannot be further mitigated or reduced by other means.”

              "According to Article 283, the paragraph 3 of the Code the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources (hereinafter – MENR) has been designated as a working body for the implementation of international treaties in the field of climate change. MENR carries out state regulation in the field of greenhouse gas emissions and removals in order to ensure the achievement of the NDC of the Republic of Kazakhstan. Moreover, under the Article 283, paragraph 4 of the Code the state agencies of the Republic of Kazakhstan, within their competence, are obliged to take actions aimed at ensuring the NDC implementation."
            ]
          }
        ],
        "priority": null
      },
      "classification_version": "2026-10-20.1"
    },

          "quote": "Achievement of NDC targets and carbon neutrality will demand holistic digitalization first of all in the energy sector and the environment to track a carbon footprint and to ensure transparency as well as the creation of an innovation ecosystem both for applied research programs and new financial tools on decarbonization.\nIntroducing intelligent systems in the power sector will touch all levels of the energy sector – systematic management, power generation, and distribution and it will enable the creation of conditions to integrate renewables (RES) and distributed generation and also strengthen the sustainability of the system due to better monitoring and maintenance.           "quote": "To ensure the achievement of NDC, it will be necessary to conduct a variety of assessment and foresight studies on the needs of the long-term low-carbon development of the Republic of Kazakhstan with the involvement of stakeholders using various methods to generate trans-disciplinary ideas.     • p. 13Text matched
      “The growing shortage of water, including due to transboundary factors, and the associated degradation of aquatic ecosystems, are among the most pressing problems for Kazakhstan. Most of the water intake goes to agriculture. Kazakhstan is also a major supplier of wheat in the region. It is expected that climate stressors such as increased droughts, changes the river flow regimes and precipitation patterns, increased temperatures, and increased occurrence of extreme weather events are expected to bring agricultural losses to the country, engendering food insecurity in the region by 2050.”

    Livestock production and traditional agro-pastoral grazing systems are expected to face significant consequences from climate variability and change. Pastures already face degradation and overgrazing and are vulnerable to desertification, droughts and storms; changing temperature, precipitation and water access could stress animals, affect growth and reproduction, and increase livestock infectious diseases.

  • Agricultural Adaptation Actions Partly UnderwayReported actions already partly undertaken include crop diversification, reduced reliance on water-intensive crops, water-saving technologies, upgraded drip irrigation, organic farming, soil management, adjusted animal fodder, and pasture protection.Underway+3 points1 document1 quote

    Agricultural adaptation actions are reported as already partially undertaken: crop diversification; moving gradually away from water-intensive crops; adopting water-saving technologies; modernizing drip irrigation and related infrastructure in response to possible changes and redistribution of annual river runoff; shifting to modern organic farming and better soil management to maintain soil carbon; changing animal fodder to reduce cattle methane emissions; preventing overgrazing; and responsibly managing and protecting pastures.

  • Sendai-Aligned Disaster Risk Work Is AdvancingKazakhstan reports progress aligned with four Sendai priorities, alongside a framework intended to mainstream adaptation and risk management and regional cooperation through a center established in Almaty in 2016.Result reported0 points1 document1 quote

    Kazakhstan reports progress implementing activities aligned with the four priorities of the Sendai Framework; its disaster-risk legislative and institutional framework is intended to mainstream climate adaptation and risk management at national and sub-national levels, with stakeholder involvement and regional cooperation through a Center for Emergency Situations and Disaster Risk Reduction established in Almaty in 2016, serving Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Afghanistan.

      “Since the adoption of the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (2015-2030) by Kazakhstan progress has been made in implementing activities aligned with the four priorities of the Sendai Framework. Nature, Forests & Land

10 claims

  • Forest Cover, Woodland, and Felling Conditions ReportedThe document reports low forest cover, distinguishes woodland and principal wood species areas, notes state ownership and cutting restrictions, and records annual felling alongside saxaul cutting and trade prohibitions introduced from 2015 and 2017.Concern0 points1 document1 quote

    Forest cover was reported as low: 12.9 million ha (4.74% of the country); shrubbery and protective plantings covered about 10 million ha, and principal wood species occupied 3.3 million ha. Satellite data showed woodlands covered 1.24% of the country, or 3.48 million ha. Nearly all forests were state-owned and protected, with restrictions on cutting. Felling removed principal wood species from 10 thousand ha per year; saxaul felling and shrub cutting cleared an additional 40 thousand ha per year. Saxaul cutting was prohibited from 2015, and the ban was extended to saxaul trade from 2017.

    • p. 12Text matched
      “Current forest cover in Kazakhstan is low: it amounts to 12.9 million ha or 4.74% of the territory. Shrubbery and protective plantings cover about 10 million hectares, while only 3.3 million hectares are occupied by principal wood species: coniferous, soft-wooded, and hard-wooded broadleaved species. Much of the area recognized as forests is not covered by woods, as confirmed by the satellite data, according to which the Kazakhstan woodlands cover just 1.24% of the total country area or 3.48 million hectares. Nearly all forests are state-owned and protected, with restrictions on cutting. Felling of principal wood species removes forest from an area of 10 thousand ha per annum. Felling of saxaul and cutting of shrubbery, registered mainly in the South of Kazakhstan, cleared some additional 40 thousand ha per annum, according to the official statistical data. Since 2015, cutting saxaul is prohibited, and from 2017 this ban was extended to the trade of saxaul.”

  • Modeled Forest Carbon Uptake and Commercial Forest BenefitsModeling through 2030 estimates carbon uptake under three scenarios, subject to stated conditions in the initial years, and describes later uptake rates and expected adaptation benefits from commercial forests.Projection0 points1 document1 quote

    The document reports modeled carbon uptake from afforestation and reforestation under three scenarios through 2030: in the first three years after planting, each hectare of the specified tree types absorbs an average of 1 ton of carbon per year (equivalent, as stated, to 3.67 tons of CO2 per hectare per year), subject to no disturbances; later the stated rate falls to 0.7 tons of carbon per forest hectare per year.     • p. 17Text matched
      “Afforestation and reforestation mitigation outcomes under three different scenarios until 2030 were modelled with the use of CBM-CFS3 (Carbon Budget Model of the Canadian Forest Sector) software. In the first three years [after planting] each hectare of coniferous, soft-wooded, or hardwood trees absorbs the average of 1 ton of carbon per year that is equivalent to 3.67 tons of CO2 per year per hectare subject to lack of disturbances. However, later this parameter drops to 0.7 tons of carbon per year per forest hectare. This can be explained by forest aging which is leading to a decrease in carbon dioxide absorption. The 25-year lifespan of commercial forests will provide the country with adaptation benefits (water retention, wood for construction, etc.) as well as increase carbon sinks offsetting anthropogenic emissions that cannot be further mitigated or reduced by other means.”

      "text": "The document reports modeled carbon uptake from afforestation and reforestation under three scenarios through 2030: in the first three years after planting, each hectare of the specified tree types absorbs an average of 1 ton of carbon per year (equivalent, as stated, to 3.67 tons of CO2 per hectare per year), subject to no disturbances; later the stated rate falls to 0.7 tons of carbon per forest hectare per year. It says commercial forests have a 25-year lifespan and describes their expected adaptation benefits and role in increasing carbon sinks. These are modeled outcomes and projections, not achieved removals.",

      "citations": [
        {
          "page": 17,
          "quote": "Afforestation and reforestation mitigation outcomes under three different scenarios until 2030 were modelled with the use of CBM-CFS3 (Carbon Budget Model of the Canadian Forest Sector) software. In the first three years [after planting] each hectare of coniferous, soft-wooded, or hardwood trees absorbs the average of 1 ton of carbon per year that is equivalent to 3.67 tons of CO2 per year per hectare subject to lack of disturbances. However, later this parameter drops to 0.7 tons of carbon per year per forest hectare. This can be explained by forest aging which is leading to a decrease in carbon dioxide absorption. The 25-year lifespan of commercial forests will provide the country with adaptation benefits (water retention, wood for construction, etc.) as well as increase carbon sinks offsetting anthropogenic emissions that cannot be further mitigated or reduced by other means."
        }
      ],

Industry & Mining

4 claims

  • Environmental Permits Require Best Available TechniquesThe Environmental Code establishes a basis for best available technologies, with comprehensive permits requiring best available techniques at significantly impactful facilities from 1 January 2025; installation is not reported.Planned action+2 points1 document1 quote

    The Environmental Code provides a basis for introducing best available technologies to reduce environmental impacts and improve resource-use efficiency. From 1 January 2025, facilities with a significant negative environmental impact are required to hold a comprehensive environmental permit requiring equipment with the best available techniques; the requirement is stated as forthcoming, not as evidence that equipment has already been installed.

    IND-01Cleaner production and industrial efficiency

    Comprehensive permit requirement begins
    1 January 2025
    Labels and conditions
    Statement type
    Planned action · p. 6
    Purpose
    Mitigation · p. 6
    Policy instruments
    Law regulation · p. 6Standard code · p. 6
    • p. 6Text matched
      “Article 113 of the Code creates a basis for the introduction of the best available technologies aimed at reducing the negative impact on the environment, minimizing and controlling the negative anthropogenic impact on the environment, improving the efficiency of the use of resources that contribute to the transition of the Republic of Kazakhstan to a green economy and low-carbon development. According to Article 418, paragraph 4 of the Code since 1 January 2025, for facilities that have a significant negative impact on the environment, it is mandatory to have a comprehensive environmental permit, which requires the use of equipment with the best available techniques.”

      “To improve water management and water use, while ensuring a stable water supply, Kazakhstan introduces basin management and integrated water resources management (IWRM) principles, implements projects increasing the coverage of the population with wastewater treatment in cities, projects implementing measures to reduce water losses during transportation in water supply networks, construction of water reservoirs, and emergency water reservoirs to catch excess rainfall, modernization and reconstruction of water canals and hydraulic structures, the introduction of modern irrigation methods and modern water-saving technologies, popularizing the use of drip-irrigation, promoting water efficiency in industry, transition to less water-intensive crops in agriculture.       "text": "To pursue decarbonization, Kazakhstan says it will need to increase renewable energy (solar and wind), make grid dispatch more adaptive, digitalize its aging energy fleet, and use digital twins. These are identified as necessary future measures.",
      "kind": "planned_action",
      "figures": [],
      "topic_ids": [

      ],
      "unmapped_concepts": [],
      "citations": [
        {
          "page": 10,
          "quote": "It will also be necessary to increase the share of renewable energy sources (solar and wind) in the balance of electricity production, and to use previously unused capacities to increase the maneuverability of the system.         }

      "page": 5,
      "quote": "the Action Plan for the implementation of the Concept for the Transition of the Republic of Kazakhstan to a \"green economy\" for 2021-2030 (Enactment of the Government of the Republic of Kazakhstan #479 dated 29 July 2020), which provides for the implementation of necessary measures to reduce greenhouse gas emissions in the energy sector, energy efficiency and energy conservation, development of sustainable transport, infrastructure for electric and gas vehicles, smart traffic management systems, sustainable municipal waste management, transition to sustainable land use methods and organic agriculture"
    },
    {
      "page": 6,
      "quote": "Since 2018, an auctioning mechanism for selecting projects of renewable energy sources (hereinafter – RES) has been introduced in Kazakhstan.     },
    {
      "page": 6,
      "quote": "According to the statement of the President of the Republic of Kazakhstan, the share of RES in electricity production is increased to 15% by 2030."
    },

    },
    {
      "page": 7,
      "quote": "hydrogen as well as other alternative sources of energy."
    },
    {
      "page": 7,
      "quote": "Action plan on implementation of the election program of the President of the Republic of Kazakhstan “Just Kazakhstan – for all and everyone, Now and forever” adopted by the Decree of the President of the Republic of Kazakhstan # 2 dated 26 November 2022 contains the following activities that contribute to achieving the NDC target by 2030: to attract by 2029 not less than 150 billion USD worth of direct foreign investment; 60% gasification of the country area; 1,5 times increase of the volume of production using RES;"
    },
    {
      "page": 7,
      "quote": "creation of a required infrastructure for EVs in large cities of the country."
    },
    {
      "page": 10,
      "quote": "41.3 percent of the population of Kazakhstan lives in rural settlements with poorly developed infrastructure, remote from industrial centers, with a small capacity of the domestic market and with a predominance of energy-intensive export-oriented sectors of the economy, which provide the main revenues of the state budget, and significantly affect economic policy and the exchange rate of the national currency. The Republic of Kazakhstan will need to introduce new and significantly strengthen existing carbon pricing mechanisms in order to achieve its NDC, which has a double dependence on fossil fuels (coal and oil) in the country."

      "text": "Monitoring progress on the NDC and carbon neutrality is described as requiring comprehensive digitalization and a climate platform providing access to emissions and pollutant information.           "page": 8,
          "quote": "The use of satellite data and intelligent systems will enable to track and monitor any changes in land use and forests and will improve the quality of data collection."

        },
        {
          "page": 8,
          "quote": "Monitoring of the NDC implementation progress will be reported in the Biennial transparency report including the progress of the current plans and programs implementation, policy and practical indicators by using available data of the unified climate platform."
